The rela-\\ntionship between the vertebral radius ( V\\nR) and DW was tested using a\\nnonparametric regression. During edge analysis, the ultimate bandwas identified (opaque or translucent) by two readers with no priorknowledge of sample size, sex or age and compared to month of cap-\\nture to determine frequency of edge type.\\nVarious growth models were fit to DW-at-age data following\\nCailliet et al.(\\n2006 ), Cotton et al.(2011 ) and Dale and Holland ( 2012 ).\\nThe von Bertalanffy growth function (VBGF) generates a growth\\ncurve that represents the predicted pattern of growth based on thefollowing equation (Von Bertalanffy,\\n1938 ):\\nDW t¼DW∞/C0DW∞/C0DW 0 ðÞ e/C0kt\\nwhere DW tis the predicted disc width at age t,D W∞is the theoreti-\\ncal maximum mean DW ( t=∞), DW 0is the estimated width at birth\\n(t=0) and k(year/C01) is the growth coefficient or the average rate at\\nwhich the organism in a population will achieve the maximum DW\\n(Cailliet & Goldman, 2004 ; Sulikowski, 1996 ).\\nTwo variations of the VBGF were also compared to determine\\nwhich model best represents the size-at-age data. Akaike informa-\\ntion criterion (AIC) analysis was used to determine which growth\\nmodel would yield the best fit for the DW-at-age data for least-squares regressions, while ML estimation used a form of AIC (AICc)\\nwith adjustment for small-sample biases (Charvet et al.,\\n2018 ; Cotton\\net al.,2011 ; Gianeti et al.,2019 ).\\n3|RESULTS\\nFemale sizes ranged from 87 to 241 mm DW (mean /C6s:d:, 191.53\\n± 22.95 mm, n=121), 153 to 448 mm TL (356.78 ± 48.97 mm,\\nn=121) and 37 to 800 g TM (472.94 ± 159.06 g, n=121). An AICc value of <2 indicated sub-\\nstantial support for the selected model (Katsanevakis &\\nMaravelias, 2008 ). Our results also indicated that for the sexes com-\\nbined the VBGF mod, VBGF 2parand the logistic models all had similar\\nparameter values for both ML- and LS-fitted models, but if selectingthe absolute lowest AICc value then the VBGF modwas best fit to the\\ndata (Table 1and Figure 7). The AICc for both ML- and LS-fitted\\nmodels indicated a best fit of the VBGF 2parfor males (Table 1and\\nFigure 7), while all models with the exception of the VBGF 2parwas\\nbest fit for the female data (Table 1and Figure 7).\\n4|DISCUSSION\\nElasmobranchs are typically characterized as having a K-selected\\ngrowth strategy, making them susceptible to fisheries and otheranthropogenic stressors, such as habitat degradation. However, the\\npresent study of yellow stingrays found them to reach sexual maturity\\nearly, produce young twice a year and have shorter lifespans thancommonly described for elasmobranch fishes. Our results, along with\\nthose of similar species, suggest a more productive life-history strat-\\negy that may be more resilient to these pressures (Torres-Palacioset al.,\\n2019 ).\\nThe sex ratio for males and females for the current study was\\nequal, with males reaching sexual maturity later than females and\\nfemales growing to larger maximum sizes than males to accommodatefor reproductive condition than males. For males, the inflexion point\\nof the CL –DW relationship was similar to the male maturity ogive\\nFIGURE 7 Selected growth curves of best-fit DW-at-age data for sexes combined, males and females. , VBGF mod(SC); , VBGF 2par\\n(M); , Gompertz (F); , male; , femaleSCHIEBER ET AL. 9\\nFISH\\n\\n(DW 50). The negligible difference between the two analyses strongly\\nsupported the size at maturity ogives, although a larger sample size\\nfor males with DW sizes between 130 and 145 mm DW remains nec-essary to rule out a smaller size at maturity. Previous studies have\\nsuggested that male yellow stingrays reach sexual maturity ca.\\n200 mm TL (Sulikowski,\\n1996 ; Yañez-Arancibia & Amezcua-\\nLinares, 1979 ). Related urotrygonids such as male Urobatis halleri\\n(Hale & Lowe, 2008 ) and U. rogersi (Mejía-Falla et al.,2012 ) have been\\nrecorded as sexually mature at 150 and 118 mm DW, respectively\\n(Table 2and Figure 8). Previous literature on female U. jamaicensis by\\nYañez-Arancibia and Amezcua-Linares ( 1979 ) and Sulikowski ( 1996 )\\nsuggests sexual maturity also peaks at ca. 200 mm TL ( ca. 116 mm\\nDW, unpublished data). Like the males, other female urotrygonids hada range of similar sizes-at-first maturity with 150 mm and 118 mm\\nDW (Hale & Lowe,\\n2008 ; Mejía-Falla et al .,2012 ) (Table 2and\\nFigure 8). Females grow slower and larger, and live longer than males\\nto accommodate the higher energetic costs of reproduction and larger\\nbrood sizes. This strategy, which is typical for viviparous elasmo-\\nbranchs, may result from a biological adaptation influenced by repro-duction rather than environmental factors (Mejía-Falla et al.,\\n2014 ).\\nDespite similar batoid species having a generally larger age-at-\\nfirst maturity estimate, yellow stingrays reaching sexual maturity\\nwithin the first year would not be unrealistic as they are a fast-grow-ing, short-lived, tropical species. The only other batoid species to our\\nknowledge with a recorded age-at-first maturity <1 year is U. rogersi ,arelated species with a proposed triannual reproductive cycle and max-\\nimum age estimates of 8 and 11 years old for males and females,\\nrespectively (Mejía-Falla et al.,\\n2014 ). Although U. rogersi is described\\nas having a triannual cycle, it may not produce three broods per year,\\nbut rather have an asynchronous cycle with three peaks per year. This\\ndifference in frequency of birth could affect the differences in maxi-mum ages achieved between the species.\\nThe positive relationship between V\\nRand DW indicated its use-\\nfulness for age-estimations, as growth of the vertebral centra\\nremained proportional with somatic growth (Dale & Holland, 2012 ;\\nMejía-Falla et al.,2014 ; Sulikowski, 1996 ). There were significant dif-\\nferences between males and females, which have been similarly\\nreported for other myliobatiform rays, with females growing larger toaccommodate reproductive condition and larger brood sizes (Almeida\\net al .,\\n2000 ; Hazin et al .,2006 ; Mejía-Falla et al .,2012 ; White\\net al .,2001 ). Mejía-Falla et al .(2012 ) noted that female Urotrygon\\nrogersi will reach larger sizes and masses than males but reach sexual\\nmaturity at a similar size and age, like Trygoptera personata (White\\net al.,2001 )o rU. jamaicensis in the current study.\\nEvidence of annual band deposition for combined size classes\\nwas inconclusive, whereas individual size classes (120 –165 mm, 166 –\\n210 mm and 211 –255 mm DW) revealed that larger yellow stingrays\\nhad more of an annual pattern of band deposition with opaquegrowth (thicker bands) during January and translucent growth (thinner\\nbands) during June and August. A species of wobbegong shark\\nfound in western Australia ( Orectolobus hutchinsi ) has similar band\\ndeposition patterns. Neonates were reported to produce up to\\nthree growth bands per year, while adults produced less than oneband per year, supporting the theory of a nonseasonal somatic\\ngrowth influence with larger vertebrae having more consistent\\ngrowth band deposition (Chidlow et al .,\\n2007 ; Huveneers\\net al .,2013 ). For yellow stingrays, there is an obvious variation in\\nband deposition rate within the first few years of life. Considering\\nthat yellow stingrays reproduce biannually with ovulation coincid-ing with parturition, energy resources allocated towards somatic\\ngrowth versus reproduction may vary greatly, especially at young\\nages where small sizes may affect mating behaviour and brood size.Typically, with the onset of maturity, the energy allocated towardsgrowth is reduced and maximum size reaches an asymptote (Mejía-\\nFalla et al.,\\n2014 ). It was noticed for yellow stingrays that maturity\\noccurs early, but growth may only slow down rather than plateauas age increases. The benefits of this strategy could influence\\nrecovery potential from the elevated mortality risks caused byhabitat changes, high predation from larger predators or fishing pres-\\nsures, including collections for the aquarium trade (Baje et al.,\\n2018 ).\\nWhen comparing the edge analysis with the reproductive cycle, March\\npeaks in ovulation during the first cycle coincided with a higher per-centage of translucent band growth, suggesting resource allocationmay be focused more towards vitellogenesis and ovulation rather than\\ngrowth. Conversely, during the second cycle, which is characterized by\\nsmaller brood sizes but larger embryos, peaks in ovulation that occurredduring August/September coincided with more opaque bands, suggest-\\ning resources may be allocated towards growth rather than vitellogene-\\nsis and ovulation. During both cycles, an increase in opaque growthoccurred during April and November, subsequent to the onset of gesta-\\ntion (Fahy,\\n2004 ,2017 ).\\nDespite the evidence of edge analysis following the biannual\\nreproductive pattern noted through the literature for yellow stingrays,\\na biannual pattern in growth band formation was not statistically evi-\\ndent for the marginal increment analysis. However, if visually asses-sing MIA, a biannual pattern of growth may be discernible, with peaksbetween February and April and again in August which coincide with\\nthe cease of ovulation in larger female stingrays. However, the trade-\\noffs of energy allocation between somatic growth and reproduction inyellow stingrays may influence the deposition of band pairs, leading to\\nnonannual growth marks along the vertebral centra.\\nFIGURE 8 Reported age-at-maturity, maximum age and female fecundity (indicated by numbers within stingray shape; NR indicates\\nfecundity not reported) for similar Myliobatid species. , male; , femaleSCHIEBER ET AL. 11\\nFISH\\n\\nThe majority of age-estimation studies may solely depend on the\\nuse of a selected ap r i o r i single model such as the original VBGF, which\\nin some cases may not be fully supported by the data or the growth tra-\\njectory of a species (Katsanevakis & Maravelias, 2008 ). The use of multi-\\nple growth models provides a more robust approach to estimates ofdifferent growth parameters that are typically unavailable, such as DW\\n0,\\nand lowers the risk of yielding biologically unrealistic growth estimates\\n(Katsanevakis & Maravelias, 2008 ;S m a r t et al.,2016 ). Size-at-age data\\nwas fit to the five different growth mo dels using the LS regression tech-\\nnique and the ML technique. Both suggest that females grow slower\\nthan males but reach larger maximum sizes, as indicated by the kand\\nDW∞values or how quickly ( k) the stingrays approach the maximum\\nmean DW (DW ∞)( O g l e , 2016 ). AICc values further suggest that the\\ntwo-parameter von Bertalanffy model best fits the male data, while the\\nGompertz model ultimately best fits the female data. Although notincluded within the present study, t he use of a multimodel inference by\\nmodel averaging based on ‘Akaike weights ’may have provided a more\\nprecise estimation of model parameters and eliminated model uncer-tainty from multiple models producing viable parameters (Katsanevakis &\\nMaravelias,\\n2008 ).\\nDespite male rays having a larger kv a l u e ,s i m i l a ro rs m a l l e rD W ∞\\nvalues were found when compared with related species. For example,\\nU. rogersi has a triannual, aseasonal reproductive pattern. To account for\\nthis pattern, Mejía-Falla et al.(2014 ) adjusted age by averaging the time\\nbetween birth and first band formation and found a two-phase growthfunction with a DW\\n∞of 155 mm and a kvalue of 0.65 year/C01.These\\nadjustments could account for the drastic differences in kvalues\\nbetween U. rogersi andU. jamaicensis . Hale and Lowe ( 2008 ) studied the\\ngrowth rates for U. halleri through wild collected samples and samples\\nheld in captivity that were injected with oxytetracycline (OTC), and\\nnoted a DW ∞of 286 mm and a kvalue of 0.09 year/C01forU. halleri .\\nAlthough U. halleri displayed annual periodicity along the vertebral cen-\\ntra with the OTC injections, growth rates could have been affected by\\ncaptivity despite constant habitat conditions (Huveneers et al.,2013 ).\\nBranstetter ( 1990 ) described growth rates as being slow if kwas\\n<1 year/C01or considerably fast if >1 year/C01, indicating that yellow sting-\\nrays would be considered a comparably fast-growing species with a\\nkvalue of 1.15 year/C01for sexes combined. Other than the obvious vari-\\nations caused by species differences, factors such as habitat type, sam-\\nple size, ageing methodology, validation method and model fitting can\\nalso lead to variation in the growth rates of closely related species(Cailliet & Goldman,\\n2004 ;S m i t h et al.,2007 ). Regardless of all these\\ninfluential factors, kcan still provide a practical characterization of the\\nrudimentary factors associated with fecundity, longevity and size or ageat maturity (Smith et al.,\\n2007 ; Stearns, 1982 ).\\nThe growth patterns and consecutive 6-month reproductive\\ncycles found for yellow stingrays may account for the variations inbirth date, a lack of age validation before the age of three, the varia-tions between MIA and edge analysis, and the large growth rate coef-\\nficient ( k) determined in the growth models. Seasonality in growth\\nband formation is typically associated with the seasonal variations inenvironmental variables such as temperature and the availability of\\nresources. Tropical elasmobranchs are generally thought to lackseasonality in growth patterns due to the constancy of the tropical\\nenvironment. Although sea water temperatures for these environ-ments can vary significantly, resource availability associated with sea-\\nsonal rainfall ( i.e., wet and dry seasons) has been considered the\\nprimary driver of phenological patterns (Green et al.,\\n2009 ). Yellow\\nstingrays seem to have higher growth during the dry winter months\\nand slower growth in the wet summer months. This seasonality in\\ngrowth for females could be due to females having increased fecun-dity, smaller embryos and slower growth during the spring/summer\\nmonths and decreased fecundity, faster growth and larger embryo\\nsizes during the fall/winter months. Larger brood sizes with smallersized offspring during the first cycle occurred during the summermonths, when water temperature was elevated (Fahy,\\n2004 ; Fahy\\net al.,2007 ). Male yellow stingrays have biannual peaks in sperm pro-\\nduction that precede the ovulatory patterns in females by 1 –2 months\\n(Fahy, 2017 ). Males are recorded more frequently in the same areas\\nas females during the post-partum/pre-ovulatory periods, follow simi-\\nlar peaks in reproductive patterns as females and thus possibly havesimilar peaks in growth patterns.\\nThe growth and reproduction patterns for yellow stingrays within\\nthis study may also be influenced by the distinct water temperaturepatterns associated with the increasing and decreasing light regime\\nfor the subtropical environment in which they were sampled. These\\ntemperature changes may influence the endocrine patterns for thisspecies, leading to the increased winter growth and decreased sum-mer growth patterns found. Further support for this hypothesis\\nincludes the composition of the vertebral bands themselves. Accord-\\ning to Green et al .(\\n2009 ), calcified opaque bands and protein-rich\\ntranslucent bands occur within fish otoliths, a hard part structure used\\nto age teleost fishes. If the opaque and translucent bands follow a\\nsimilar composition to that of fish otoliths, then the protein-rich trans-lucent bands occurring most often during yellow stingray peak ovula-\\ntion could explain the thin bands occurring during the spring and\\nsummer months when fecundity is highest.\\nThe yellow stingray is a small, fast-growing urotrygonid that\\nreaches more than 40% of asymptotic size by birth and attains an esti-\\nmated maximum of 5 and 6 years of age for males and females,\\nrespectively. Although males and females have similar sizes at matu-rity, males grow faster and mature at a younger age, whereas females\\ngrow slower but achieve larger maximum sizes. The annual periodicity\\nof band pairs could only be verified with marginal increment analysisand edge analysis for larger stingrays. These patterns support rapid\\ngrowth through the first few years of life, followed by slower, more\\nconsistent growth as age and size increased. These patterns suggestgrowth rates are most likely attributed to nonannual somatic growth\\nrather than seasonality. Growth estimates for both male and female\\nstingrays yielded large kvalues and small DW\\n∞estimates, which are\\nboth consistent with a short-lived, fast-growing tropical batoid. Con-sidering only seven of the 20 known species within the Urotrygonidae\\nfamily have sexual maturity and age information available, the results\\nof this study can be used to fill in the knowledge gaps for similar spe-cies. The age and growth data collected from this study could also be\\nused as a proxy for ecosystem-based management decisions of similar12 SCHIEBER ET AL.\\nFISH\\n\\nsmall, tropical, or fishery-impacted batoid, as well as providing a\\ndiverse outlook for data-deficient species or species that may displaya nonannual or nonseasonal somatic growth pattern.\\nAUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS\\nAll persons who meet authorship criteria are listed as authors. Though Labour and the Conservatives slightly outperform their vote share in terms of seats under STV, smaller parties’ seat share in our model is much more similar to how people actually voted at the election, with the Liberal Democrats making significant gains in our projection (an additional 48 MPs, leading them to have 9.3% of seats on 11.8% of the vote)."}]}', error=None), ToolExecutionRecord(tool_name='fetch_url_text', caller_message_id='run--80069871-82ae-4c6b-a5d6-2f42ba0ff2d9-0', tool_message_id='6238c22c-bef5-4c1f-932e-518f475d899c', tool_call_id='toolu_01Bm29pzvDWpmgz6qVSfdYgv', arguments={'url': 'https://electionresults.parliament.uk/elections/1792'}, result='{"text": "[Skip to main content](https://electionresults.parliament.uk/elections/1792#main-content)\\n[ ](https://www.parliament.uk/)\\n  1.
